chunks: First: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadala from Dawud ibn Farqad from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever eats this food, let him not approach our mosque,' meaning garlic, and he did not say it is forbidden.

Second: From him, from Muhammad ibn Abi Umayr from Umar ibn Udhayna from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: I asked him about garlic, and he said: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) only forbade it because of its smell, and said: 'Whoever eats this bad vegetable, let him not approach our mosque.' As for whoever eats it and does not come to the mosque, there is no harm.

Third: From him, from Hammad ibn Isa from Shu'ayb from Abu Basir said: Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) was asked about garlic, onions, and leeks, and he said: There is no harm in eating them raw or cooked in the pot, and there is no harm in being treated with garlic, but when one of you eats that, let him not go out to the mosque.
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on eating garlic and onions before going to the mosque?
ai.summary: These narrations from al-Istibsar clarify that the consumption of garlic, onions, and leeks is permissible (halal) and not inherently impure, with the restriction being a recommendation (mustahabb) to avoid approaching the mosque to preserve its spiritual atmosphere. The scholars distinguish between the prohibition of entering the mosque with the odor and the permissibility of eating them raw or cooked, emphasizing that the aversion is due to the strong smell affecting others rather than a ritual impurity (najis) of the food itself. This ruling highlights the Shia emphasis on social etiquette (adab) and communal harmony within sacred spaces.
